arXiv:2509.04903v1 [cs.CL] 05 Sep 2025

ACE-RL: Adaptive Constraint-Enhanced Reward for Long-form Generation Reinforcement Learning

Jianghao Chen Wei Sun Qixiang Yin Lingxing Kong Zhixing Tan Jiajun Zhang ††thanks: Corresponding Author
Abstract

Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable progress in long-context understanding, yet they face significant challenges in high-quality long-form generation. Existing studies primarily suffer from two limitations: (1) A heavy reliance on scarce, high-quality long-form response data for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or for pairwise preference reward in reinforcement learning (RL). (2) Focus on coarse-grained quality optimization dimensions, such as relevance, coherence, and helpfulness, overlooking the fine-grained specifics inherent to diverse long-form generation scenarios. To address this issue, we propose a framework using Adaptive Constraint-Enhanced reward for long-form generation Reinforcement Learning (ACE-RL). ACE-RL first automatically deconstructs each instruction into a set of fine-grained, adaptive constraint criteria by identifying its underlying intents and demands. Subsequently, we design a reward mechanism that quantifies the quality of long-form responses based on their satisfaction over corresponding constraints, converting subjective quality evaluation into constraint verification. Finally, we utilize reinforcement learning to guide models toward superior long-form generation capabilities. Experimental results demonstrate that our ACE-RL framework significantly outperforms existing SFT and RL baselines by 20.70% and 7.32% on WritingBench, and our top-performing model even surpasses proprietary systems like GPT-4o by 7.10%, providing a more effective training paradigm for LLMs to generate high-quality content across diverse long-form generation scenarios. 11 1 Our code is available at https://github.com/ZNLP/ACE-RL

1 Introduction

Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) have yielded significant improvements in their long-context understanding capabilities (Google 2025; OpenAI 2024a; Anthropic 2025; Yang et al. 2025a). This success has naturally pushed the research frontier towards a more challenging field: high-quality long-form generation (e.g., storytelling, report writing, or legal document drafting). However, generating coherent, well-structured, and engaging content over thousands of words still remains a significant and unresolved challenge for current long-context LLMs (Wu et al. 2025b; Bai et al. 2025; Wu et al. 2025c).

While many researchers focus on supervised fine-tuning (SFT) (Bai et al. 2025; Pham, Sun, and Iyyer 2024), these approaches are often constrained by reliance on costly synthetic datasets from proprietary LLMs and a lack of optimization for response quality attributes (Deng, Kuleshov, and Rush 2022; Pham, Sun, and Iyyer 2024). In contrast, reinforcement learning (RL) alleviates this by enabling direct optimization of desired qualities through a reward mechanism. This allows for a more flexible and robust approach to training models for long-form generation, particularly when focusing on specific human preferences. However, existing RL-based methods primarily rely on pairwise preference reward with coarse-grained evaluation dimensions (Lei et al. 2025; Wu et al. 2025a). As shown in Figure 1, while these methods ensure fundamental qualities such as relevance, coherence, and helpfulness, they fall short of addressing the detailed, instruction-adaptive demands of diverse tasks. For example, given a storytelling instruction: “Write a 3000-word novel about a young, struggling couple with an O. Henry-style ending." The core of the instruction is the writing style of a surprise, ironic twist, a quality that is not a universal marker of “good" writing, but a highly specific stylistic demand. Moreover, the reliance on extra preference response pairs imposes a significant data collection burden, making the process both costly and difficult to scale.

To address the above issue, we propose a framework with Adaptive Constraint-Enhanced reward for long-form generation Reinforcement Learning (ACE-RL). The core innovation of ACE-RL lies in its training paradigm shift away from coarse-grained, subjective rewards toward fine-grained, verifiable rewards. Specifically, our framework begins by employing an automated pipeline to collect and analyze diverse long-form generation instructions from real-world human-LLM interactions. This pipeline deconstructs each instruction by identifying both its explicit demands and implicit intents, converting them into a checklist of verifiable constraints. We then introduce a novel reward mechanism that scores a generated response based on its satisfaction over these constraints. This process effectively transforms the subjective challenge of evaluating writing quality into a series of constraint verification tasks. Finally, by leveraging reinforcement learning guided by this fine-grained reward signal, ACE-RL significantly enhances the long-form generation capability of LLMs.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We propose ACE-RL, a novel reinforcement learning framework that utilizes fine-grained, instruction-adaptive rewards for long-form generation.

  • •

    We introduce an automatic pipeline for constructing long-form generation instructions with constraint checklists, and we will release our datasets for future studies.

  • •

    We design a novel reward mechanism that transforms subjective quality evaluation of long-form responses into constraint verification tasks.

  • •

    Extensive experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms SFT and RL baselines, and even surpasses strong proprietary LLMs.

2 Related Work

2.1 Long-context Understanding for LLMs

The enhanced long-context understanding capabilities of LLMs have significantly broadened their application across various fields, such as long-chain reasoning (Yeo et al. 2025; Chen et al. 2025a; Yang, Liao, and Fan 2025), long video and image processing (Guo et al. 2025b; Jian et al. 2025; Jian, Yu, and Zhang 2024), and agent interaction (Zhang et al. 2024; Ren et al. 2025; Xu et al. 2025). Recent studies have proposed both model-centric and data-centric methods. Model-centric methods involve novel model architectures (Gu and Dao 2024; Dao and Gu 2024; Peng et al. 2023), efficient attention (Liu et al. 2024; Lu et al. 2025; Shah et al. 2024), and extrapolation of positional encoding (Xiong et al. 2024; Peng et al. 2024; Ding et al. 2024; An et al. 2024a). These approaches focus on redesigning the core components of LLMs to handle extensive contexts more efficiently and effectively. In parallel, data-centric methods improve the long-context ability of LLMs through continual pre-training (Fu et al. 2024; Chen et al. 2024a; Chen et al. 2025b) or supervised fine-tuning (Bai et al. 2024; An et al. 2024b; Chen et al. 2024b). However, these studies mainly focus on long-context input scenarios, and generating high-quality long-form outputs remains a significant challenge for current LLMs.

2.2 Long-form Generation for LLMs

The challenge of long-form generation has been approached primarily from two directions: supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. SFT-based methods focus on data synthesis, such as long-form response construction (Quan et al. 2024; Bai et al. 2025) and instruction back-translation (Pham, Sun, and Iyyer 2024). Recent success of reinforcement learning with preference reward (Sun, Shen, and Ton 2025; Yang et al. 2025b) encourages researchers to explore outcome-based RL for long-form generation. Lei et al. (2025) leverage proprietary LLMs to generate reference responses and calculate pairwise reward by quality comparison of model responses and reference responses. Wu et al. (2025a) utilize a reward model trained with preference data pairs to capture general response quality such as fluency, coherence, and helpfulness.

However, these approaches rely on coarse-grained rewards with extra preference data pairs, failing to capture the fine-grained, instruction-specific details that define high-quality writing in diverse scenarios. Therefore, we propose the ACE-RL framework, which utilizes a novel reward mechanism with fine-grained, instruction-adaptive constraint verification.

3 Methodology

This section details the framework of our proposed ACE-RL, a novel approach for improving the long-form generation capabilities of LLMs. As illustrated in Figure 2, the core innovation lies in systematically breaking down each high-level user instruction into a checklist of fine-grained constraints. This process transforms the abstract goal of “writing a good response" into a set of concrete, verifiable objectives, enabling us to construct a precise reward signal that directly reflects the model’s ability to meet specific user demands.

3.1 Data Preparation

The rapid development of LLMs has led to the emergence of numerous high-quality datasets, laying a solid foundation for building powerful LLMs (Penedo et al. 2024; Chen et al. 2023).To construct a high-quality dataset tailored for long-form generation, we collect a diverse set of long-form generation instructions from WildChat-1M (Zhao et al. 2024), a large-scale dataset of real-world human-LLMs interactions. We first conduct deduplication to remove redundant instructions. Then, we employ Qwen3-235B-A22B (Yang et al. 2025a) to filter out instructions that specifically call for long-form generation. Furthermore, considering that adherence to length constraints is a critical aspect of long-form generation tasks, we augment each instruction with the target word count by leveraging Qwen3-235B-A22B for analysis. Detailed prompts are provided in Appendix A.

3.2 Adaptive Constraint Construction

Long-form generation instructions are often open-ended and under-specified, requiring models to not only address explicit requests but also to infer and fulfill a wide range of implicit expectations related to logical flow, depth of analysis, and completeness. Therefore, to facilitate fine-grained, adaptive evaluation of such tasks, ACE-RL employs a pipeline that automatically deconstructs a high-level user instruction into a checklist of verifiable constraints. This procedure transforms the ambiguous goal of a long-form generation instruction into a set of concrete, measurable objectives that can directly guide the RL process. We employ Qwen3-235B-A22B for constraint checklist generation, ensuring consistency with our data preparation stage.

Given an instruction, we prompt the LLM to act as an instruction analyst. The model identifies both the explicit requirements directly stated by the user and the implicit expectations beyond the literal instruction. These requirements are then reformulated into a series of clear, distinct, and verifiable items to form a complete constraint checklist. For instance, a user request for a detailed disk topology design (Figure 3) contains explicit requirements (highlighted in red) that can be directly extracted. Furthermore, the implicit expectation, like effective topology for future expansion (highlighted in green), is also important for a comprehensive answer. Therefore, by identifying and integrating both explicit and implicit constraints, this procedure provides a robust foundation for reward modeling and ensures the RL process is tightly aligned with the specific demands of users. The detailed prompt and cases of instruction-checklist pairs are provided in Appendix A and Appendix B, respectively.

3.3 Reward Design and RL Training

The design of the reward function is crucial for guiding policy model optimization during RL training. Recent studies often employ LLM-as-a-Judge for evaluating the quality of long-form outputs (Lei et al. 2025; Wu et al. 2025a). These approaches typically use abstract, holistic quality evaluation derived from pairwise preference comparisons. Such methods remain subjective, coarse-grained, and fail to capture the fine-grained, specific demands of user instructions. Our reward mechanism is designed to overcome these limitations. We utilize the satisfaction of model responses over the corresponding constraint checklists as the reward signals, providing a more fine-grained and concrete guidance for the policy optimization process. We provide details of the algorithm and reward design for RL training as below.

Training Algorithm

We adopt the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al. 2024) algorithm for RL training. GRPO removes the additional value model from PPO (Schulman et al. 2017) and instead calculates the advantages through group comparison. Given a specific query qq from training dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D}, GRPO sample GG rollouts {o1,…,oG}\{o_{1},\dots,o_{G}\} from the old policy model πθold\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}} and calculate their rewards {R1,…,RG}\{R_{1},\dots,R_{G}\}. Then the advantage AiA_{i} of each rollout is estimated by comparing each RiR_{i} with the average reward of this group. The final optimization objective of GRPO is defined as follows:

ri=πθ​(oi∣q)πθold​(oi∣q),riclip=clip⁡(ri,1−ε,1+ε)\displaystyle r_{i}=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(o_{i}\mid q)}{\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(o_{i}\mid q)},\,r_{i}^{\mathrm{clip}}=\mathrm{clip}(r_{i},1-\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon) (1)
Ai=Ri−mean⁡({R1,…,RG})std⁡({R1,…,RG})\displaystyle A_{i}=\frac{R_{i}-\operatorname{mean}(\{R_{1},\dots,R_{G}\})}{\operatorname{std}(\{R_{1},\dots,R_{G}\})} (2)
𝒥⁡(θ)\displaystyle\mathcal{J}(\theta) =𝔼q∼𝒟,{oi}i=1G∼πθold(⋅∣q)\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mathcal{D},\{o_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}\sim\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(\cdot\mid q)} (3)
[1G∑i=1G(min(riAi,riclipAi)−βDKL(πθ∥πref))]\displaystyle\Biggl[\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\Bigl(\min(r_{i}A_{i},r_{i}^{\mathrm{clip}}A_{i})-\beta D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})\Bigr)\Biggr]

where rir_{i} is the importance sampling ratio, ε\varepsilon is the clip threshold, β\beta controls the penalty strength of KL divergence, and πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} is the fixed reference policy model.

Length Reward

In long-form generation, meeting a specified length is often a key requirement. Existing LLMs tend to provide too short responses or fall into endless repetition (Bai et al. 2025). Therefore, we introduce a length reward to control the generation length for the response of the policy model. Given an instruction with target length LtL_{t} and a rollout response y^\hat{y}, we define the follwing length reward RL​(y^)R_{L}(\hat{y}):

δ=|Ly^−Lt|Lt\displaystyle\delta=\frac{\lvert L_{\hat{y}}-L_{t}\rvert}{L_{t}} (4)
RL​(y^)={1.0δ≤Δexp(−α⋅(δ−Δ))δ>Δ\displaystyle R_{L}(\hat{y})=\begin{cases}1.0&\delta\leq\Delta\\ \exp\left(-\alpha\cdot\left(\delta-\Delta\right)\right)&\delta>\Delta\end{cases} (5)

where δ\delta is the relative length deviation, Δ\Delta is the allowable relative deviation threshold, and the decay factor α\alpha controls the degree of length penalty. One rollout response will get a maximum reward of 1.0 if its length falls within an acceptable range of the target length. If the length deviates beyond this range, the reward would decrease exponentially.

Constraint Reward

To evaluate whether one rollout response meets each item in the generated constraint checklist, we employ a verifier LLM. Specifically, given an instruction I​n​s​tInst, its corresponding constraint checklist {c1,c2,…,cN}\{c_{1},c_{2},\dots,c_{N}\} and policy model response y^\hat{y}, the verifier model is prompt to output a three-level judgment: "Fully Met" if the response completely satisfies the constraint; "Partially Met" if the response addresses the constraint to some extent but is incomplete or contains minor errors; "Not Met" if the response fails to address the constraint. This transforms the subjective evaluation for long-form outputs into a series of constraint verification tasks, where utilizing the long-context understanding capability to guide the enhancement of the long-form generation ability of LLMs. We define the constraint reward RC​(y^)R_{C}(\hat{y}) as following:

s⁡(y^,ci)=fLLM​(T,I​n​s​t,y^,ci)∈{0,0.5,1}\displaystyle s(\hat{y},c_{i})=f_{\mathrm{LLM}}(T,Inst,\hat{y},c_{i})\in\{0,0.5,1\} (6)
RC​(y^)=1N​∑i=1Ns⁡(y^,ci)\displaystyle R_{C}(\hat{y})=\frac{1}{N}\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{N}s(\hat{y},c_{i}) (7)

where s⁡(y^,ci)s(\hat{y},c_{i}) is the score for one rollout response y^\hat{y} to instruction I​n​s​tInst on constraint cic_{i}, which is determined by the verifier LLM fLLMf_{\mathrm{LLM}} with prompt template TT. The verifier LLM outputs a score from {0,0.5,1}\{0,0.5,1\}, corresponding to the three-level judgments: "Fully Met", "Partially Met", and "Not Met". The overall constraint reward is then calculated as the mean of all individual constraint scores. Through RL training, this reward signal guides the policy model to align its responses with the fine-grained, multifaceted demands of the user instructions. The prompt template used for verifier LLM is shown in Appendix A.

Overall Reward

The overall reward R⁡(y^)R(\hat{y}) is defined as the average of the length reward and the constraint reward:

R⁡(y^)=12​(RL​(y^)+RC​(y^))\displaystyle R(\hat{y})=\frac{1}{2}\Bigl(R_{L}(\hat{y})+R_{C}(\hat{y})\Bigr) (8)

4 Experimental Settings

4.1 Training Dataset

We conduct RL training on long-form generation instruction datasets constructed in Section 3. Each instruction is paired with a checklist of constraints and a length requirement. Table 1 shows the detailed statistics of our training dataset.

4.2 Training Configuration

We perform RL training under the VERL (Sheng et al. 2025) framework with the GRPO algorithm. We split 480 samples to construct a validation set and train each model for 200 steps, using a batch size of 64, a rollout number of 32, and a learning rate of 1×10−61\times 10^{-6}. To accommodate long-form generation, we set the maximum generation length to 8192 and use a sampling temperature of 1.0. For length reward, we set the relative deviation threshold Δ\Delta to 0.2 and the decay factor α\alpha to 0.5. For constraint reward, we utilize Qwen3-8B (Yang et al. 2025a) for constraint verification. We also remove the KL penalty term following recent studies (Yu et al. 2025).

4.3 Baselines

We compare ACE-RL with the following methods:

Current Leading LLMs

We evaluate: (1) Proprietary LLMs: o3-2025-04-16 (OpenAI 2025), Gemini-2.5-pro-preview-06-05 (Comanici et al. 2025), Claude-3.7-sonnet (Anthropic 2024b), GPT-4o (OpenAI 2024a), o1-Preview (OpenAI 2024b). (2) Open-source LLMs: Deepseek-R1 (Guo et al. 2025a), Qwem-3 series LLMs (Yang et al. 2025a), Qwen-2.5 series LLMs (Yang et al. 2024), Llama-3 series LLMs (Dubey et al. 2024). (3) Writing-enhanced LLMs: LongWriter-llama3.1-8B, LongWriter-glm-9B (Bai et al. 2025), LongWriter-Zero-32B (Wu et al. 2025a).

Long-form Generation SFT

We perform SFT on LongWriter dataset following Bai et al. (2025).

LLM-as-a-Judge RL

Since our method does not require pairwise preference data for training, we adapt the LLM-as-a-Judge prompt (removing pair comparison) from (Lei et al. 2025) for RL training. To ensure a fair comparison, the same Qwen3-8B model is employed for LLM-as-a-Judge as is used in our ACE-RL constraint verification.

4.4 Evaluation Benchmarks

WritingBench

contains 1000 diverse long-form writing instructions over 6 major domains and 100 sub-domains (Wu et al. 2025d). Each instruction is paired with several evaluation criteria of three dimensions: style, format, and length. The final evaluation is conducted by a fine-tuned critic LLM, achieving over 80% agreement with human judgments.

Arena-Write

comprises 100 real-world user writing queries with six strong baseline responses for comparison (Wu et al. 2025a): DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al. 2025a), Qwen2.5-72B (Yang et al. 2024), GPT-4o (OpenAI 2024a), GLM-Z1-32B (GLM et al. 2024), Claude-3.5-Sonnet (Anthropic 2024a), and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B (Guo et al. 2025a), resulting in a total of 600 comparisons. We follow all its evaluation settings with Qwen3-235B-A22B as the judge model and calculate the winning rate of model responses against these six baselines.

5 Results and Analysis

We assess ACE-RL with both non-thinking LLMs Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B/7B (Yang et al. 2024) and thinking LLMs Qwen3-1.7B/4B (Yang et al. 2025a) across WritingBench, Arena-Write, and human evaluation.

5.1 Main Results

As illustrated in Table 2, we provide the detailed performance of diverse LLMs over WritingBench. LLMs trained with our ACE-RL framework significantly outperform baseline methods across all domains and requirements. Specifically, our trained Qwen-2.5-7B-instruct achieves an overall score of 78.57, significantly surpassing its original model (57.04), SFT method (62.11), and LLM-as-a-Judge RL method (70.28). For reasoning models, our trained Qwen-3-4B-thinking even shows better performance, with an average score of 82.56, outperforming scores of the original one (72.43) and LLM-as-a-Judge RL baseline (79.65). These substantial improvements underscore the critical role of our instruction-adaptive reward mechanism in boosting the long-form writing capabilities of LLMs. We present cases of thinking processes and responses in Appendix C.

Notably, our method proves highly competitive even when compared with leading proprietary systems and specialized writing models. Our Qwen-3-4B-thinking model (82.56) not only outperforms proprietary LLMs like Claude-3-7-sonnet (78.48) and GPT-4o (74.46), but also surpasses writing-enhanced models like LongWriter-Zero-32B (80.30), LongWriter-llama3.1-8B (58.01), and LongWriter-glm-9B (62.94). Moreover, we discover that model scale is not the primary determinant of long-form generation quality. Even our trained Qwen-2.5-1.5B-instruct models (75.68) can achieve higher performance than Qwen-2.5-72B-instruct (65.28) and Llama-3.3-70b-instruct (50.43), suggesting that a better training paradigm may be more critical to unlock better long-form generation performance.

To further validate our method, we report the pairwise “win-tie-loss" rate of our models against six baselines on the Arena-Write benchmark. As shown in Table 3, our method demonstrates a decisive advantage in preference evaluations. Our trained Qwen-3-4B-thinking model achieves a remarkable win rate of 67.73% when compared with six strong baselines, including larger-scale models or proprietary systems, underscoring the success of our ACE-RL framework in unlocking the long-form generation capability of LLMs.

5.2 Superiority of RL over SFT

A consistent trend across all model scales is the superior performance of RL-based methods over SFT-based methods. Notably, even the Qwen-2.5-1.5B model trained with ACE-RL can achieve an average score of 75.68, significantly surpassing the 62.11 score of the much larger Qwen2.5-7B model with LongWriter SFT. This result underscores the critical role of the training paradigm in long-form generation. The effectiveness of SFT is inherently constrained by the quality and scope of its static training dataset. Any shortcomings or biases in the SFT data, such as a domain gap between the synthetic examples and the complexity of real-world scenarios, would directly constrain the model’s performance ceiling. In contrast, RL-based training allows the model to move beyond simple imitation. By learning a policy through exploration and reward, the model develops a more robust and generalizable understanding of the task, enabling it to generate higher-quality outputs that are better aligned with complex, real-world objectives.

5.3 Effectiveness of Test-Time Scaling

Test-time scaling has been demonstrated to improve performance on reasoning tasks (Guo et al. 2025a). To investigate whether these benefits extend to long-form generation, we conduct comparative experiments on Qwen-3-1.7B using two modes: “thinking" and “non-thinking". In the “thinking" mode, our training paradigm guides the model to first analyze the user’s intent and then create a structured plan or chain of thought before generating the final response. In contrast, the “non-thinking" mode involves direct, single-pass generation of the response. The results, presented in Table 4, indicate that the explicit internal reasoning process leads to the generation of higher-quality content, thereby yielding significantly better performance than the “non-thinking" approach. We present the complete results in Appendix D.

5.4 Effectiveness of Reward Design

While LLM-as-a-Judge is a promising approach for guiding long-form generation, current methodologies present significant challenges in terms of cost, scalability, and reliability. For example, Wu et al. (2025a) train a Qwen2.5-72B reward model on manually-labeled preference data pairs, and Lei et al. (2025) utilize Qwen-Plus (Yang et al. 2024) for pairwise comparison during RL training. Such methods introduce substantial cost and limit scalability due to dependency on additional labeled data. Furthermore, recent work shows that LLMs’ judgment exhibits preference biases, causing the reward for both high-quality and low-quality responses to cluster within a narrow range (Li et al. 2025). This lack of discriminatory power is evident in Figure 4, where the reward distribution within groups from an LLM-as-a-Judge shows substantially lower variance than that of our ACE-RL method. This suggests that LLMs’ judgment based on general dimensions like coherence, relevance, and helpfulness can not distinguish responses of different quality. In contrast, our method converts the coarse-grained, subjective evaluation of long-form responses into fine-grained constraint verification tasks, enhancing the efficiency and reliability of reward generation with small-scale models.

5.5 Impact of Reward Model

To further investigate the efficiency of our method, we conduct RL training with reward models of different scales. As shown in Table 5, our Qwen-2.5-1.5B-instruct model guided by Qwen-3-4B reward model (71.30) outperforms the LLM-as-a-Judge approach with a larger Qwen-3-8B reward model (61.25). Furthermore, our method excels even in a self-reward setting: our Qwen-4B-thinking model trained on its own reward signals (81.76) surpasses the LLM-as-a-Judge baseline that relies on an 8B reward model (79.65). These results demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our reward mechanism through constraint verification. The success of the self-reward setting showcases the potential for LLMs to bootstrap their own improvement without the need for larger, external judge models. We present the complete results with different reward models in Appendix D.

5.6 Human Evaluation

To mitigate biases inherent in automated evaluation, we conduct human evaluation with real-world instructions from the Arena-Write benchmark. We compared Qwen-3-4B trained with ACE-RL against its base model and the LLM-as-a-Judge RL method. As shown in Figure 5, our method consistently achieves higher win rates, demonstrating its superiority in aligning with human preferences.

6 Conclusion

This paper introduces ACE-RL, a novel and efficient reinforcement learning framework to enhance the long-form generation capability of LLMs. ACE-RL leverages an effective reward mechanism that measures the quality of long-form responses via instruction-adaptive constraints verification. By converting coarse-grained, subjective evaluation to fine-grained verification tasks, LLMs trained with ACE-RL demonstrate their superiority over other SFT and RL methods, and even surpass leading proprietary LLMs. ACE-RL offers new pathways for a verifiable reward-based RL paradigm for long-form generation scenarios.
